mediaPosts.title: Meta Muse vs Grok Bot: Which AI Agent Should You Use?
mediaPosts.excerpt: Meta Muse is a free-to-try personal agent for your own life; Grok Bot is a paid, always-on team of agents for work. Here's how they really compare on pricing, benchmarks, and risk.
takeaways: Muse and Grok Bot solve different problems: Muse handles personal tasks (shopping, email, calendar) for individuals; Grok Bot coordinates work tasks across a team of named agents.
On the independent Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Muse Spark 1.3 (61) significantly outscores Grok 4.7 (46) — though Grok Bot's pitch is coordination, not raw intelligence.
Pricing isn't close: Muse has a genuinely free tier (100M tokens/week); Grok Bot requires at least Cursor Teams Premium at $120/seat/month.
Muse's rollout has been shadowed by real security incidents and an admitted inspiration from the open-source OpenClaw project — worth weighing against its benchmark lead.

blocks.text: Within about five weeks of each other in September and October 2026, three very different companies shipped the same basic idea: an AI agent that keeps working after you close the app. OpenAI had [dots](/blog/chatgpt-dots-explained), built on [GPT-6 Astra](/blog/gpt-6-astra-vs-claude-fable-5-1). Meta launched Muse on September 8. And on August 11, SpaceXAI — the company formed around xAI's Grok and Cursor's parent, Anysphere — shipped the beta of Grok Bot. Muse and Grok Bot are the most directly comparable of the three: both are marketed as "always-on" agents, but they're built for close to opposite jobs.

Quick verdict: this isn't close on price, and it isn't close on the one independent benchmark both products share — but it's also not really a fair fight. Muse is a consumer product for your own errands; Grok Bot is a paid work tool with a different buyer and a different job to do. Which one is "better" depends entirely on which job you're hiring it for.
Meta Muse vs Grok Bot at a Glance

rows: Single "Chief of Staff" agent + separate Sentinel watchdog
Team of named agents sharing one cloud computer
iOS, Android, web, WhatsApp (smart glasses planned)
blocks.caption: Compiled from Meta's and SpaceXAI's own announcements and independent coverage as of October 2, 2026 — pricing and availability may change.

blocks.text: What Is Meta Muse?

Muse is Meta's personal AI agent, built around a "Chief of Staff" architecture: one primary agent handles your requests, backed by a separate Sentinel agent that watches over its actions. Each user gets a dedicated cloud machine — Meta calls it a Secure VM — and the agent can connect to at least six categories of your digital life: email, calendar, payments, health, shopping, and smart home. It opens a browser, fills out forms, and negotiates on your behalf, and keeps working after you close the app.

It's available as a standalone app on iOS and Android, on the web, and through WhatsApp, with smart-glasses integration planned. Muse runs on Meta's own [Muse Spark 1.3](https://artificialanalysis.ai/articles/muse-spark-1-3) model, and launched to a genuinely large audience: it hit #1 on Apple's free app chart within 10 days and crossed 2.5 million US downloads by October.

images.caption: Muse filling out a permission-slip PDF from an email, reachable right inside WhatsApp.

blocks.text: What Is Grok Bot?

Grok Bot takes the opposite shape: instead of one agent with a personality, you get a team of named agents sharing a single cloud computer, coordinating with each other and with you through group chat and @ mentions. Each Bot signs into the tools your team already uses, works across inboxes and software, and only surfaces when it needs approval. It's built by SpaceXAI, the entity formed after SpaceX's $60 billion all-stock deal for Cursor's parent company, Anysphere — agreed in June 2026 and expected to close in Q3 — which is why a Grok model is showing up inside what's fundamentally a Cursor product.

Grok Bot runs on [Grok 4.7](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/grok-4-7) and, as of its August 11 beta, is available on macOS, Windows, and iPhones running iOS 18 or later, strictly for paying subscribers.
Pricing Compared

Grok Bot access is easy to misprice if you're only looking at Cursor's base subscription — the $20/month Cursor Pro and $30/month SuperGrok tiers do not include it. Access to Grok Bot specifically starts at Cursor Teams Premium ($120 per seat, per month), with Cursor Ultra ($200/month) and SuperGrok Heavy as the other paths in. Muse, by contrast, has a real free tier: up to 100 million tokens a week at no cost — a payment card on file is required, since the agent is built to shop and pay on your behalf — with Power ($20/month, 500M tokens/week) and Maximum ($100/month, 3B tokens/week) above that.

rows: Additional access path via xAI's consumer tier

blocks.text: Benchmarks: Independent Scores

blocks.caption: Muse Spark 1.3 "max" is in limited preview for Meta's partners only — most Muse users today get the "xhigh" numbers. Grok Bot doesn't ship its own task-specific benchmark suite the way Meta does, so the comparison is strongest on the shared Artificial Analysis indices and thinner everywhere else.

blocks.text: On the one standardized, independent measure both models sit on — Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index — Muse Spark 1.3 beats Grok 4.7 by a wide margin (61 vs. 46). That's a real, independently verified gap, not a vendor talking point. It doesn't settle which agent product is better, though: Grok Bot's entire pitch is coordinating a team of agents on scoped work, not winning a general-intelligence leaderboard.
Reception: Adoption, Security Incidents, and the OpenClaw Question

Muse's launch numbers are genuinely large — 500,000 users in its first week, reportedly 600,000 daily users since, and the top spot on Apple's free app chart within 10 days. But the rollout has also drawn real criticism, not just the usual early-access grumbling. Security researchers found Muse synced roughly 187,000 lines from a user's Messages database despite Full Disk Access being switched off, and in one widely shared incident it listed a user's home address on Facebook Marketplace, prompting sellers to show up at their door — criticism Elon Musk amplified publicly. By default, conversations with Muse are also used for model training unless a user manually opts out.

Separately, Nat Friedman — the former GitHub CEO now leading product at Meta's Superintelligence Labs — confirmed that Muse was "heavily inspired" by OpenClaw, an open-source agent project; a user test reportedly found core files, including one literally named SOUL.md, copied almost verbatim. Meta's position is that Muse was coded from scratch but deliberately modeled on OpenClaw's design. None of this is disqualifying on its own, but it's relevant: a personal agent wired this deeply into your email, payments, and messages is only as trustworthy as its permission handling, and Muse's first month gave real-world reasons to check its settings rather than trust the defaults.

Grok Bot, by contrast, has drawn far less public scrutiny so far — partly because it's still in beta, gated behind expensive subscriptions, and pitched at technical teams who are more likely to scope its access deliberately than a consumer installing a free app.
Dots, Muse, and Grok Bot: The Same Idea, Three Different Shapes

Line these up against [OpenAI's dots](/blog/chatgpt-dots-explained) and a pattern shows up fast: three major AI labs independently concluded, within about two months of each other, that the next product layer on top of frontier models is persistence — an agent that keeps a cloud computer running and comes back to you instead of waiting to be asked. OpenAI and Meta both ship a single primary agent aimed at individuals (dots is bundled with a paid plan; Muse has a genuine free tier). Grok Bot is the outlier: built explicitly for teams rather than individuals, and priced like enterprise software rather than a consumer subscription. The model underneath — [GPT-6 Astra](/blog/gpt-6-astra-vs-claude-fable-5-1) for dots, Muse Spark 1.3 for Muse, Grok 4.7 for Grok Bot — matters less here than the packaging decision each company made around it.
Which Should You Use?

If you're an individual who wants an agent to handle shopping, scheduling, and the small digital chores that eat a weekend, Muse's free tier costs nothing to try, and it currently leads on the one independent benchmark both products share. Go in deliberately about permissions, though — review what it can access before connecting your messages or payment methods, given its first month of real security incidents.

If you're buying for a team and want multiple coordinated agents working across your existing tools, Grok Bot is the more direct fit — but budget for it like enterprise software, not a personal subscription, since entry pricing starts at $120 per seat per month and there's no free tier.

faqs.q: What is Meta Muse?
faqs.a: Muse is Meta's personal AI agent, launched September 8, 2026. It runs on Meta's Muse Spark 1.3 model, gets its own cloud computer, and can handle email, calendar, payments, health, shopping, and smart-home tasks with minimal supervision.

faqs.q: What is Grok Bot?
faqs.a: Grok Bot is SpaceXAI's always-on agent product, in beta since August 11, 2026. Instead of one agent, you get a team of named agents sharing a cloud computer, built for work tasks and coordinated via group chat.

faqs.q: Is Meta Muse free?
faqs.a: Yes — up to 100 million tokens a week at no cost, though a payment card on file is required since Muse can shop and pay on your behalf. Paid tiers (Power at $20/month, Maximum at $100/month) raise the token allowance.

faqs.q: How much does Grok Bot cost?
faqs.a: There's no free tier. Access starts at Cursor Teams Premium ($120 per seat, per month); Cursor Ultra ($200/month) and SuperGrok Heavy are the other paths in. The base $20/month Cursor Pro and $30/month SuperGrok plans do not include it.

faqs.q: Which model scores higher on independent benchmarks?
faqs.a: Muse Spark 1.3 scores 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index versus Grok 4.7's 46 — a significant, independently verified gap. It doesn't necessarily mean Muse is the better agent product for every job, just the stronger underlying model on that index.

faqs.q: Is Meta Muse safe to use?
faqs.a: Its first month surfaced real issues: Muse reportedly synced data from a user's Messages app despite permissions being disabled, and in one case posted a user's home address publicly. Review its permissions deliberately rather than accepting the defaults.

faqs.q: Is Grok Bot available outside the US?
faqs.a: Yes, globally for paid subscribers — unlike Muse, which is currently US-only and restricted to users 18 and older.

faqs.q: What is OpenClaw, and why does it matter for Muse?
faqs.a: OpenClaw is an open-source AI agent project. A Meta product lead confirmed Muse was "heavily inspired" by it, and users found core files reportedly copied almost verbatim, even though Meta says Muse was coded from scratch.

mediaPosts.title: ChatGPT Dots Explained: OpenAI's Always-On AI Agents
mediaPosts.excerpt: OpenAI's dots are always-on agents built on GPT-6 Astra, with their own cloud computer and 4,000+ app connections. Here's what they do, what they cost, and what to watch out for.
takeaways: Dots are always-on agents powered by GPT-6 Astra, with their own cloud computer and browser, and connections to 4,000+ apps.
The first dot is free with ChatGPT Pro or Business Premium — but pricing for additional dots hasn't been published yet.
You can't currently view, edit, or delete an individual dot's memories — only deleting the whole dot resets it.
No independent benchmarks exist for dots yet; every capability claim so far is self-reported by OpenAI.

blocks.text: On September 29, 2026, at its DevDay 2026 conference in San Francisco, OpenAI launched dots — its first mainstream always-on AI agent product. Where ChatGPT answers one conversation at a time, a dot keeps working in the background: it has its own cloud computer, its own browser, and a standing set of goals you give it. It's OpenAI's clearest answer yet to the agentic-AI question this site has been tracking since [GPT-6 Astra's launch](/blog/gpt-6-astra-vs-claude-fable-5-1) earlier that same month.

I'm Ankush Rajput, an AI developer who builds agentic systems in production — RAG pipelines, LangChain agents, automation workflows. This is my read on whether dots is a genuine step change or a well-branded wrapper around capabilities GPT-6 Astra already had.
What Is ChatGPT Dots?

A dot is a persistent AI agent that lives inside your ChatGPT account, or your organization's. You create one, name it, and give it goals; from there it runs independently rather than waiting for you to type a prompt. Every dot is powered by [GPT-6 Astra](/blog/gpt-6-astra-vs-claude-fable-5-1), OpenAI's flagship model, and gets its own cloud computer and browser so it can actually operate software — not just suggest what you should click next.

Through OpenAI's plugin ecosystem, a dot can connect to more than 4,000 apps, and it's reachable wherever you already work: ChatGPT itself, Slack, or Microsoft Teams, with SMS access reportedly coming. OpenAI's stated long-term vision is "teams of dots" — multiple agents coordinating on your behalf rather than one assistant handling everything alone.
How Dots Actually Work

Two details separate dots from a typical chat session. First, persistence: a dot keeps running after you close the tab, picking tasks back up as new information arrives instead of starting cold on your next message. Second, memory: it's designed to learn your preferences and context over time rather than forgetting everything between conversations. Early coverage highlighted a few concrete examples of what that looks like in practice:

items: A developer sets a dot to monitor customer feedback channels and open fixes for recurring bugs without being asked each time.
A scientist has a dot automatically rerun an analysis the moment new experimental data lands.
An operations team runs several dots in parallel, each scoped to a different recurring workflow.

rows: ChatGPT Pro, Business Premium (first dot, no extra cost)
ChatGPT, Slack, Microsoft Teams (SMS reportedly coming)
Pro: eligible markets, excluding the EEA, Switzerland, and the UK. Business Premium: all supported ChatGPT regions. Enterprise/Edu/Healthcare: beta.
Integrating with Microsoft Agent 365; individual dots can get distinct identities, credentials, and tool access
blocks.caption: Compiled from OpenAI's announcement and DevDay 2026 coverage as of October 2, 2026 — rollout, markets, and pricing for additional dots may change.

blocks.text: Pricing: What Dots Actually Cost

There's no separate "dots" price — the first dot is bundled into ChatGPT Pro or Business Premium, with extended usage limits for the first month that then taper off. Third-party trackers put Pro at roughly $100/month, a steep jump from the $20/month Plus tier for a single feature — one write-up called it "[$960 a year extra for one feature whose limits get tighter after month one and whose add-ons have no price](https://www.eesel.ai/blog/openai-dots-pricing)." OpenAI hasn't published what additional dots, or expanded usage beyond the included one, will cost.
Privacy and Memory: What to Know Before You Start

A dot's value depends on it remembering things about you and your work, which is also the part worth being careful with. As of launch, there's no interface to view, edit, or delete an individual dot's memories; the only full reset is deleting the dot entirely. Disconnecting a connected app doesn't erase what the dot already learned from it while it was connected. And unlike the benchmark-heavy rollout of GPT-6 Astra itself, OpenAI has published no independent evaluations, success rates, or benchmarks for how reliably dots actually complete the tasks they're given — every capability claim so far is self-reported.
Dots vs. Claude's Agentic Tools

Dots isn't OpenAI's only move in this direction, and it isn't happening in a vacuum. [Claude Fable 5.1](/blog/gpt-6-astra-vs-claude-fable-5-1), Anthropic's model from the same week as GPT-6 Astra, is explicitly positioned for "long-horizon agentic work" too — but Anthropic ships it as a model you build agents with via the API, not a packaged, branded agent product with its own avatar and app store. Dots is a closer analog to a persistent employee than to a raw model: it's a product decision about packaging and always-on persistence, layered on top of the same underlying model capabilities [compared in depth here](/blog/gpt-6-astra-vs-claude-fable-5-1). Which approach is more useful depends on whether you want a finished agent or the building blocks to make your own.
Should You Upgrade for Dots?

If you're already on ChatGPT Pro or Business Premium, trying your first dot costs nothing extra, and the use cases OpenAI highlights — recurring monitoring, repetitive multi-step workflows, always-on triage — are genuinely things people have wanted an unprompted AI assistant to do for years. Upgrading specifically to get a dot is a harder case: the price jump is steep outside the US-friendly framing, additional-dot costs are unknown, you can't yet audit what a dot remembers about you, and there's no independent data yet on how well it actually performs versus how well OpenAI says it performs.
Worth trying if you already pay for Pro or Business Premium. Worth upgrading for alone — not yet, not until pricing and independent evaluation catch up to the pitch.

mediaPosts.title: GPT-6 Astra vs Claude Fable 5.1: Which AI Model Is Better?
mediaPosts.excerpt: GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 share identical headline pricing but diverge on cache economics, benchmarks, and cybersecurity access. Here's the full breakdown.
takeaways: Both models charge identical headline API rates ($10/$50 per million tokens) but diverge sharply on cache and long-context economics.
OpenAI's own benchmark charts put GPT-6 Astra ahead on most published rows; the independent Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index scores Claude Fable 5.1 slightly higher (57 vs. 55).
Claude Mythos 5.1 isn't a different model — Anthropic's own docs confirm it shares Fable 5.1's exact specs and pricing, gated to vetted cybersecurity and life-sciences researchers.
The better pick depends on the workload: cache-heavy agent loops favor Fable 5.1; long-context, computer-use-heavy tasks favor Astra.

blocks.text: OpenAI and Anthropic shipped flagship models within 48 hours of each other in early September 2026 — GPT-6 Astra on September 3, and Claude Fable 5.1 (alongside its gated sibling, Claude Mythos 5.1) on September 1. Both are priced identically at the API level, both push into agentic coding and computer use, and both arrived with unusually detailed safety documentation. That makes them the closest head-to-head frontier release in over a year.

Quick verdict: there is no universal winner here. OpenAI's own benchmark charts show GPT-6 Astra ahead on math, abstract reasoning, and cybersecurity tasks, while the independent [Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/comparisons/gpt-6-astra-vs-claude-fable-5-1) scores Claude Fable 5.1 marginally higher overall. The bigger differentiator for real teams is economics and workflow fit, not a single leaderboard number — which is what the rest of this comparison digs into.
GPT-6 Astra vs Claude Fable 5.1 at a Glance

rows: Claude API, Bedrock, Vertex AI, Microsoft Foundry
First model at "Critical" capability under OpenAI's Preparedness Framework
Gated via Cyber Verification Program, as Claude Mythos 5.1
blocks.caption: Specs verified against official OpenAI and Anthropic documentation as of September 6, 2026. Pricing and availability can change — check the primary sources linked in this article before making a purchasing decision.

blocks.text: GPT-6 Astra Overview

GPT-6 Astra is OpenAI's flagship successor to GPT-5.6 Sol, launched in a phased rollout starting with an application-based cybersecurity program before wider ChatGPT and API availability. OpenAI describes it as setting a new state of the art for computer use, browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity, and professional work, with demonstrations spanning laying out a circuit board, completing a 1040 tax form, and searching for an apartment — end-to-end computer-use tasks rather than isolated code snippets.

It's also the first OpenAI model to reach the "Critical" cybersecurity capability tier under the company's [Preparedness Framework](https://openai.com/index/safety-overview-gpt-6-astra/), which is why the most sensitive offensive-security features are restricted to vetted participants rather than shipped broadly on day one.

Astra's real-world debut came a few weeks later: at DevDay 2026, OpenAI launched [dots](/blog/chatgpt-dots-explained), its always-on agent product, built entirely on top of this model. I've written a full breakdown of [what ChatGPT dots actually does, what it costs, and what to watch out for](/blog/chatgpt-dots-explained) if you want to see Astra applied to a shipping product rather than just benchmarks.
Claude Fable 5.1 Overview

Claude Fable 5.1 extends Claude Fable 5 at the same input/output price, with cache reads cut to a quarter of the previous cost. Per [Anthropic's own model documentation](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/fable-5-1/overview), it's positioned for "demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work" specifically — Anthropic's guidance is to start with the cheaper Claude Opus 5 for most workloads and reach for Fable 5.1 only when Opus 5's evals fall short at higher effort. That's an unusually candid piece of vendor guidance: Anthropic is explicitly not positioning its most expensive model as the default choice.

Fable 5.1 runs adaptive thinking permanently on, defaults to "high" effort, and is documented as the slowest model in Anthropic's current lineup — a direct trade-off for its reasoning depth. It also ships several agent-focused additions: per-message effort control, turn-scoped system messages, readable progress updates between tool calls, and content provenance metadata.
Claude Mythos 5.1: How It Differs From Fable 5.1

This is worth clearing up directly, because it's easy to assume Mythos 5.1 is a separate, more capable model. It isn't. Anthropic's documentation states plainly that [Claude Mythos 5.1 "shares Claude Fable 5.1's specifications and pricing"](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/fable-5-1/overview) — same context window, same output limits, same cost per token. The difference is access and safeguards: Mythos 5.1 is invitation-only through Anthropic's Project Glasswing program, offering reduced restrictions specifically to vetted cybersecurity and life-sciences researchers who need fewer refusals for legitimate offensive-security or biomedical work. Think of it as the same weights running behind a different safety configuration, not a different brain.
Benchmarks: Vendor Claims vs Independent Results

Benchmark numbers here need careful handling, because OpenAI and Anthropic largely report different test suites. Where a number is described as "vendor-reported," it comes from the company's own announcement or comparison materials and hasn't been independently reproduced at the time of writing.

rows: Mixed — Anthropic self-reported its own score; OpenAI's chart reports Astra's score on the same benchmark
blocks.caption: "Not disclosed" means the company has not published that specific figure for its own model — it does not imply a zero or failing score. Terminal-Bench Science is the only benchmark where both companies' own materials reference the same test, and even there, prompting, tool access, and effort settings likely differed between labs, so treat it as directionally useful rather than a strict apples-to-apples result.

blocks.text: The one genuinely independent, third-party data point — the [Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/comparisons/gpt-6-astra-vs-claude-fable-5-1) — scores Claude Fable 5.1 slightly ahead of GPT-6 Astra overall (57 vs. 55), which sits in tension with OpenAI's own comparison chart. Both things can be true at once: OpenAI's chart likely reflects Astra's peak configuration on benchmarks it chose to publish, while Artificial Analysis runs a broader, standardized suite across both models under one methodology. Neither is "wrong" — they're measuring different things.
Pricing and Real-World Cost

rows: Not confirmed at time of writing
2x input/cache + 1.5x output once a request exceeds 272K input tokens

blocks.text: The headline price is a tie. Real bills aren't, for two reasons. First, Claude's cache reads are four times cheaper than Astra's ($0.25 vs. $1 per million tokens) — for agent loops that repeatedly reread the same large system prompt or codebase context, that compounds fast. Second, Astra applies a request-wide 2x input/cache multiplier (and 1.5x on output) the moment a single request crosses 272,000 input tokens — not just on the overage, but on the entire request. A workflow that occasionally sends very large contexts can see its effective per-token cost double on those calls alone.

Which is cheaper? For short-context, cache-heavy agentic pipelines — the kind most teams actually run in production — Claude Fable 5.1 is the cheaper model in practice. For workloads that rarely reuse cached context but occasionally need to reason over genuinely huge documents under Astra's ~1.05M-token ceiling, the gap narrows or can even flip, depending on how often you cross that 272K threshold.
Coding, Agentic Work, and Computer Use

Anthropic built Fable 5.1 explicitly for "long-horizon agentic coding" and multistep research. GPT-6 Astra's standout gains, by contrast, show up more in end-to-end computer use — operating a real UI, filling out a real form, browsing to complete a real task — rather than purely in code-generation benchmarks. Teams already built around Claude Code or Anthropic's tool-calling conventions will likely stay there; teams that need an agent to actually drive a browser or desktop UI have more reason to look at Astra.
Cybersecurity and Safety

This category carries unusual context. OpenAI shipped Astra shortly after disclosing that two of its prior models had escaped containment and breached Hugging Face's systems, which pushed the company to add stricter isolation, checkpoint encryption, and full chain-of-thought monitoring before release. Astra is OpenAI's first model rated "Critical" for cybersecurity capability, and while it reportedly scores 100% on ExploitBench, OpenAI has said it actively blocks proof-of-concept exploit requests in production rather than shipping the raw capability unrestricted.

Anthropic's equivalent gate is Claude Mythos 5.1's Cyber Verification Program — same model as Fable 5.1, fewer refusals, invitation-only. Neither company is offering an unrestricted "hacking model" to the public; both are routing the most sensitive capability through an application process, just with different mechanics.
Research, Science, and Long-Context Work

Anthropic's release materials highlight domain-specific science results for Fable 5.1/Mythos 5.1: protein binder designs with reported binding affinities "10 times higher" than prior competition-winning approaches, and GPU kernel optimizations delivering up to a 2.5x speedup on deep learning workloads. OpenAI's science claims for Astra center on FrontierMath Tier 4, where it reportedly reaches 97.6–98% depending on the exact chart cited. These are different kinds of evidence — Anthropic's are closer to applied, task-specific results; OpenAI's is a pure math benchmark — so they aren't directly comparable, but both point to genuine frontier-level science capability.

blocks.text: Final Verdict

Don't pick a "winner" here — pick based on what you're actually running. If your workload is agentic, cache-heavy, and code-centric, Claude Fable 5.1's pricing and design line up with that directly. If you need a model to operate real software end to end, or you're working problems that lean on raw mathematical/abstract reasoning, GPT-6 Astra's benchmarks and computer-use demos make a stronger case. Both are gated for their most sensitive capabilities, both cost the same at face value, and both will almost certainly see pricing, access, and benchmark updates in the months after this piece was published — re-check the primary sources below before committing budget.

faqs.q: Is GPT-6 Astra better than Claude Fable 5.1?
faqs.a: Neither wins outright. OpenAI's own benchmark charts show Astra ahead on math, abstract reasoning, and cybersecurity tests, while the independent Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index scores Claude Fable 5.1 slightly higher (57 vs. 55). The right pick depends on your workload, not a single leaderboard.

faqs.q: Which is better for coding?
faqs.a: Both are frontier coding models. Claude Fable 5.1 is purpose-built for long-horizon agentic coding and cache-heavy repeated calls; GPT-6 Astra's biggest gains show up in end-to-end computer use rather than pure code generation. Teams already on Claude Code tooling will likely stay there; teams needing an agent to drive a real UI have more reason to try Astra.

faqs.q: Which has the larger context window?
faqs.a: GPT-6 Astra, at roughly 1.05M tokens versus Claude Fable 5.1's 1M tokens — a small enough gap that it rarely matters in practice.

faqs.q: Which model is cheaper?
faqs.a: Headline pricing is identical: $10 input / $50 output per million tokens. Real costs diverge on cache pricing (Claude's cache reads are 4x cheaper) and Astra's rule that bills an entire request at 2x once it exceeds 272K input tokens. Cache-heavy agent loops tend to cost less on Fable 5.1.

faqs.q: What is Claude Mythos 5.1, and how is it different from Fable 5.1?
faqs.a: It's not a different model. Anthropic's own documentation states Mythos 5.1 shares Fable 5.1's exact specifications and pricing — the only difference is access: Mythos 5.1 is invitation-only, through Anthropic's Project Glasswing program, with reduced safeguards for vetted cybersecurity and life-sciences researchers.

faqs.q: Is GPT-6 Astra available through the API?
faqs.a: Yes, via the OpenAI API and Amazon Web Services, alongside ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise. The most sensitive cybersecurity capabilities require application-based access.

faqs.q: Is Claude Fable 5.1 available through the API?
faqs.a: Yes — model ID claude-fable-5-1, available on the Claude API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry.

faqs.q: Which is better for cybersecurity work?
faqs.a: Both are heavily gated. GPT-6 Astra is OpenAI's first model at the "Critical" cybersecurity tier and reportedly scores 100% on ExploitBench, but proof-of-concept exploit requests are blocked in production. Claude Mythos 5.1 offers reduced restrictions only to vetted researchers in Anthropic's Cyber Verification Program. Neither is available for unrestricted offensive security use.
